Forgotten figures

Mamie and Kenneth Clark: the doll test

A study with black and white dolls that reached the US Supreme Court.

In the 1940s, the psychologists Mamie Phipps Clark and Kenneth Clark showed African American children two dolls identical except for skin colour. They asked which one they wanted to play with, which was "the nice one" and which looked like them.

What they found

Most preferred the white doll and attributed negative traits to the black one. Some became upset when asked which one looked like them. The Clarks interpreted this as an effect of segregation on children's self-esteem.

Their work was cited in the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling, which declared school segregation unconstitutional in the United States. Mamie Clark, whose master's thesis started the research, also founded a children's centre in Harlem. For years her role was overshadowed by her husband's.

References

  1. Clark, K. B. y Clark, M. P. (1947). Racial identification and preference in Negro children. En T. M. Newcomb y E. L. Hartley (eds.), Readings in Social Psychology. Holt.
